theme: We have not forgotten you, communal lament
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 44. This is a corporate lament, the prayer of a whole people who feel abandoned by God even though they have been faithful. Notice that the psalm does not confess a sin. Read it with those who suffer innocently.
settingTheScene: Psalm 44 is a psalm of the sons of Korah. It reflects a time of national defeat: the army has been routed, the people scattered, and the nation mocked. We do not know the exact occasion. It fits any period of national humiliation, and it has been prayed by God’s people in many centuries. Here, in the age of the divided kingdom, it gives voice to the faithful in a time of judgment.
observation: “O God, we have heard with our ears, our fathers have told us, what deeds you performed in their days” (v. 1).
“For not by their own sword did they win the land, nor did their own arm save them, but your right hand and your arm” (v. 3).
“In God we have boasted continually, and we will give thanks to your name forever” (v. 8).
“But you have rejected us and disgraced us and have not gone out with our armies” (v. 9).
“You have made us like sheep for slaughter and have scattered us among the nations” (v. 11).
“All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you, and we have not been false to your covenant” (v. 17).
“Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” (v. 22).
“Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord? Rouse yourself! Do not reject us forever!” (v. 23).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with memory. The people recall what God did for their ancestors in the conquest. They know that victory was God’s gift, not their own achievement. This is the foundation of their confidence: God has acted before.

Then comes the shock of verse 9, marked by the word “But.” The God who gave them victory has now rejected them. The psalm describes the defeat in blunt terms. The army is routed. The people are sold for nothing. Neighbors mock. The psalmist feels deep shame.

The most striking feature is the claim of innocence. “All this has come upon us, though we have not forgotten you.” Unlike many laments, there is no confession of sin. The people say that they have been faithful. Whether this is a claim of perfection or a statement about their covenant loyalty in general, the psalm expresses the experience of suffering that is not explained by wrongdoing. The Bible allows for this. Not every hardship is a punishment. Sometimes the righteous suffer, and the psalm lets them say so.

The language of the closing verses is bold. “Awake! Why are you sleeping, O Lord?” It is not irreverence. It is the language of covenant. The people are saying, “You promised to be with us. Where are you?” They have no explanation, only an appeal: “Redeem us for the sake of your steadfast love.” The final plea rests on God’s character. It is not their merit but his covenant love that gives them hope.

Verse 22 is quoted by Paul in Romans 8:36, and he applies it to the experience of believers: “For your sake we are killed all the day long.” He then declares, “In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.” The psalm’s question is answered in Christ.
connection: Paul quotes verse 22 in Romans 8:36 and answers the psalm’s cry with the assurance that nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Romans 8:37-39). Jesus is the Lamb led to slaughter (Isaiah 53:7; Acts 8:32). 2 Corinthians 4:8-11 describes the suffering of the faithful. Jesus himself cried, “Why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), taking the experience of abandonment on himself.
application:
If you are suffering though you have been faithful, pray this psalm. God hears the cry that does not explain.

Recall what God has done for your ancestors in faith, and tell it to someone younger.

Read Romans 8:31-39 alongside this psalm and hold both.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what he has done in days of old that you cling to.
Ask him to rise up and help.
Thank him that nothing can separate you from his love.
